title: Introduction to matrix-product states and tensor networks
abstract: These notes provide an introduction to tensor-network methods in quantum many-body physics, with an emphasis on matrix-product states (MPS). They develop the basic tensor-network language, including graphical notation, virtual indices, bond dimensions, gauge freedom, canonical forms, QR and singular-value decompositions, and the role of entanglement in controlling the efficiency of the representation. The main MPS algorithms are then introduced, including contractions, correlation functions, matrix-product operators, DMRG, and time-evolution methods. The notes also briefly discuss projected entangled-pair states (PEPS) as a higher-dimensional generalization of MPS, together with the basic ideas behind approximate PEPS contraction. Finally, tensor-network representations of mixed states, quantum channels, and Lindblad dynamics are presented, with applications to thermal states and open quantum systems. The presentation is accompanied by short Julia code examples based on ITensor, ITensorMPS, and TensorMixedStates. These notes were written for the 9th Les Houches Summer School on Computational Physics: Open Quantum Systems, held in June 2026.
summary: This comprehensive set of notes introduces tensor networks, focusing heavily on Matrix-Product States (MPS), as a computational tool for quantum many-body physics. It details the mathematical machinery required—including entanglement measures and canonical forms—to simulate ground states, time evolution, and open system dynamics efficiently. The work is essential reading for anyone using numerical methods to study strongly correlated or dissipative quantum matter.
main_problem: To provide a comprehensive introduction to tensor-network (TN) methods, particularly Matrix-Product States (MPS), for efficiently simulating quantum many-body systems.
main_result: TNs offer a powerful framework that encodes the entanglement structure of a state, allowing polynomial scaling simulations for states obeying an area law, which is crucial for 1D and low-dimensional quantum physics.
method: The paper develops the mathematical language of TNs (graphical notation, bond dimensions) and details core algorithms like DMRG, time evolution methods (tDMRG/TEBD), and generalizations to PEPS for higher dimensions.
model_or_system: The notes cover a wide range of systems, including 1D quantum spin chains, open quantum systems governed by Lindblad dynamics, classical statistical mechanics models, and general quantum circuits.
key_observables: Entanglement Entropy ($S_{vN}$), Bond Dimension ($\chi$), Magnetization $\langle\sigma^z_{N/2}angle$, and the steady state density matrix $ho_{ss}$.
important_parameters: Bond dimension ($\chi$) controls accuracy vs. cost; the area law dictates efficient representability.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the physical state or dynamics can be accurately captured by a low-rank tensor decomposition (i.e., obeying an area law).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate MPS structures, PEPS generalizations to 2D lattices, and graphical representations of elementary tensor operations like contractions and SVD.
paper_structure: The structure progresses logically from defining the basic TN language and MPS for 1D systems, through core algorithms (DMRG/time evolution), generalizing to higher dimensions (PEPS), and finally applying the formalism to open quantum systems and mixed states.
why_interesting: This is highly relevant as it provides a complete methodological toolkit for simulating dynamics in complex, interacting quantum systems, directly applicable to modeling decoherence or non-equilibrium steady states in AMO physics.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

Each box (or circle) represents a tensor, and each leg represents an index of the tensor. In this representation the open legs (labeled s1, . . . , sN) that are not connected to any other tensor represent the physical indices. Figure 5: Construction of an MPS from a vector representation by successive QR decompositions. At each step, the Q matrix gives an MPS tensor A[i], while the R matrix is reshaped and factorized again at the next site. Such a construction leads to an MPS in a left-canonical gauge (see Fig. 8).

Figure 6: Partial contractions of a left-canonical MPS and a right-canonical MPS. For each value of the open virtual index αn, the left contraction defines a state |αn⟩L in the Hilbert space of the first n sites, while the right contraction defines a state |αn⟩R in the Hilbert space of sites n + 1, . . . , N. The corresponding canonical conditions imply that these states form orthonormal families. See also Fig. 8.
